title: Unwell newborn with suspected early-onset sepsis
desc: This station involves a focused history from the midwife and mother and an A to E examination of a 14-hour-old term baby who has become unwell, then interpreting the reassessment, blood gas, blood count, CRP and chest X-ray, outlining the management of early-onset sepsis with shock with doses for this baby, and safety-netting the family.
stem: You are the junior doctor called to the postnatal ward to review a 14-hour-old baby, born at 38+5 weeks with a birth weight of 3.2 kg. The midwife is concerned because the baby has become unsettled, is feeding poorly and is breathing noisily. The mother is at the bedside. The midwife will assist you and give observations when asked.
tasks: Take a focused history from the midwife and the mother and perform a focused examination of the baby using an A to E approach, telling the examiner what you are examining and why. Call for any help you need (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you a reassessment of the baby and the first investigation results. Interpret them, then outline your management approach, with doses for this baby, and your safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Roles: the postnatal ward midwife and the mother (one student can voice both, or the examiner voices the midwife). The baby is in a cot under a warmer. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings when the candidate says what they would examine. The midwife gives the observations and a BGL when asked.

This is an acute station. If the candidate asks for help during Part 1 (calling the neonatal team, oxygen, IV access, a BGL), the midwife says she is doing it and the candidate carries on with the assessment. How the baby responds is given in Part 2. If the candidate has not called for help by halfway through Part 1, the midwife says: "I'm really worried about this baby. Who else should we call?"

Midwife's opening line: "Thanks for coming so quickly. The baby is 14 hours old, has stopped feeding properly and has started grunting. The baby just doesn't look right to me."

Midwife, when asked:

  • Born at 38+5 weeks by normal vaginal birth. Apgar scores 9 and 9, no resuscitation needed. Birth weight 3.2 kg. Vitamin K and hepatitis B vaccine given.
  • Breastfed well twice in the first few hours. Since about 10 hours of age the baby has been sleepy and unsettled, with only brief attempts at the breast and a weak suck.
  • Fast breathing and grunting started about 2 hours ago. No pauses in breathing or blue episodes seen so far.
  • Felt hot to touch in the last hour.
  • Passed urine once and meconium once. One small milky vomit, never green.
  • Mother: GBS positive on the vaginal and rectal swab at 36 weeks. Her waters broke at home 20 hours before the birth, and she came in once contractions started. Labour was quick, and she had one dose of IV benzylpenicillin 2 hours before the birth. Her temperature was 38.2 °C in labour. The liquor was clear and not offensive.
  • The pregnancy was otherwise normal: normal scans, no diabetes, normal antenatal bloods.

Mother, when asked:

  • "The baby was feeding well this morning, but now won't latch and feels hot and floppy."
  • This is your second baby. Your first child is well. You are well yourself now.
  • You thought the baby was just tired after the birth.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you are frightened the baby will die, and you wonder whether something you did in labour caused this. You want to keep breastfeeding and to stay with the baby.

Questions to ask if there is time: "Is my baby going to be all right?" "Did I cause this?"
guide:
In Part 1, the midwife and mother answer the history and the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. This is an acute station: credit calling for help, oxygen and access whenever the candidate asks for them, in Part 1 or Part 2. In Part 2, hand over the results and ask the questions in order.

A high-performing candidate recognises sepsis with shock quickly, calls the neonatal team early, checks the BGL, finds every maternal risk factor, gives oxygen and a 32 mL bolus, takes a blood culture and gives benzylpenicillin and gentamicin with correct doses without delay. They interpret the gas, neutropenia, early CRP and chest X-ray correctly, plan neonatal unit care with a 36-hour antibiotic review, speak to the mother with honesty and empathy, and give specific safety netting including late-onset GBS and future pregnancies.

A borderline candidate recognises that the baby is unwell but escalates late, misses the BGL or a risk factor, cannot give doses, is reassured by the low CRP, or gives a limited explanation and vague safety netting.
explain:
Early-onset neonatal sepsis

Early-onset sepsis (in the first 48 hours in the RCH guideline; some definitions use 72 hours) is usually from maternal flora, most commonly Group B streptococcus and E. coli. Risk factors include maternal GBS carriage, inadequate intrapartum antibiotics (less than 4 hours before birth), prolonged rupture of membranes (18 hours or more), maternal fever and prematurity. This baby has four of them.

Recognition and stabilisation

Signs include grunting, tachypnoea, tachycardia, poor perfusion (CRT 3 seconds or more), temperature instability, lethargy and poor feeding. Call the neonatal team early. Give oxygen for the low saturations (91% here), titrated to the target range the neonatal team uses for a term baby, obtain IV or IO access, give a 10 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus (32 mL for 3.2 kg) and reassess, check the BGL, take a blood culture and give antibiotics without delay. The RCH Neonatal antimicrobial guidelines use benzylpenicillin and gentamicin for early-onset sepsis; the Australasian Neonatal Medicines Formulary doses for a term baby in the first week are benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg 12-hourly (192 mg) and gentamicin 5 mg/kg 24-hourly (16 mg). If meningitis is suspected or the CSF is abnormal, the RCH guideline uses benzylpenicillin with a third-generation cephalosporin instead. Maintenance fluid in the first day is 10% glucose (RCH Neonatal intravenous fluids), 60 mL/kg/day for a term baby (8 mL/h).

Interpreting the results

The reassessment shows a response to oxygen and fluid, but the baby is still unwell. The metabolic acidosis (pH 7.24, bicarbonate 17 mmol/L, base excess -9) with a lactate of 4.2 mmol/L reflects poor perfusion; the pCO2 of 40 mmHg shows the fast breathing is compensating for now, and a rising pCO2 on a repeat gas would mean the baby is tiring. Neutropenia in a septic newborn is a worrying sign. CRP rises over 12 to 24 hours, so a low early value does not exclude sepsis. The chest X-ray fits pneumonia; GBS pneumonia can look like surfactant deficiency. Blood culture is the key test, and a lumbar puncture is done once the baby is stable.

Disposition and safety netting

The baby needs neonatal unit care. Escalate apnoea, a rising oxygen need, recurrent shock after two boluses, hypoglycaemia or seizures. Antibiotics are reviewed at 36 hours with the culture result: the RCH guideline stops them then only if the cultures are negative and the baby is well, which is unlikely for a baby with shock, neutropenia and pneumonia. The mother is supported to stay close and provide breast milk. Before discharge, parents are told the signs of late-onset infection, which can occur in the first 3 months, and, if GBS infection is confirmed, the mother is offered antibiotics in labour in any future pregnancy.
points: Treat suspected early-onset sepsis urgently: blood culture, then benzylpenicillin and gentamicin (RCH Neonatal antimicrobial guidelines, doses from the Australasian Neonatal Medicines Formulary), without delaying treatment.
Shock in a neonate (HR above 160, CRT 3 s or more, raised lactate; a low BP is a late sign) needs a 10 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus with reassessment and a BGL check.
A normal early CRP does not exclude sepsis; repeat it, and review antibiotics at 36 hours with the cultures and the baby's condition.
Communicate honestly with the mother, reassure that GBS carriage is common, and support breast milk expression and bonding.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self to the mother and midwife, and works in a calm, organised way.
Uses plain language with the mother, acknowledges her fear and keeps her informed.
History
Characterises the illness:

kids.x: Onset of sleepiness, poor feeding and a weak suck from about 10 hours of age
Fast breathing and grunting, and any pauses in breathing or colour change
Urine and meconium passed, and vomiting (whether green)

check.x: Identifies the risk factors for early-onset sepsis:

kids.x: Intrapartum antibiotics given less than 4 hours before birth (inadequate)
Membranes ruptured 18 hours or more before birth (20 hours)

check.x: Asks about the birth and the baby's condition after it: gestation, mode of birth, Apgar scores and any resuscitation, and feeding method.
Explores the mother's ideas, concerns and expectations.
Examination
Observes colour, tone, activity and cry: pale, mottled, floppy, weak cry, responds to voice only.
Assesses breathing: RR 74, grunting, recession and nasal flaring; asks for SpO2 (91% in room air) and listens to the chest (fine crackles at the bases).
Assesses circulation: HR 188, central CRT 4 seconds, cool mottled peripheries, weak peripheral pulses and BP 58/30.
Checks the BGL straight away and states that 4.1 mmol/L is normal (2.6 mmol/L or above).
Measures the temperature (38.1 °C), undresses the baby fully and checks the fontanelle, skin for rash, umbilicus, abdomen, tone and primitive reflexes.
Interpretation

Recognises sepsis with shock and respiratory distress from Part 1: HR above 160, CRT 3 seconds or more, mottling, a systolic BP of 58 (just below the newborn range; BP falls late), grunting, low SpO2 (91% in room air), fever and reduced responsiveness.

Interprets the reassessment: the baby has responded to oxygen and one bolus (SpO2 95%, HR 164, CRT 2 seconds) but remains unwell and needs close reassessment, with a further bolus if shock signs return.
Interprets the gas as a metabolic acidosis with a raised lactate (pH 7.24, base excess -9, lactate 4.2) from poor perfusion.
Interprets the blood count: a low white cell count and neutropenia support sepsis and are a worrying sign, and the platelets are slightly low.
States that a CRP barely above normal this early does not exclude sepsis, as CRP rises over 12 to 24 hours, and plans a repeat.
Interprets the chest X-ray as consistent with pneumonia (GBS pneumonia can look like surfactant deficiency) and names the likely diagnosis: early-onset sepsis, probably GBS, with pneumonia.
Considers other causes: transient tachypnoea or surfactant deficiency, duct-dependent congenital heart disease, and an inborn error of metabolism, and says that none should delay antibiotics.
Management
Calls the neonatal registrar or NICU team early, using a structured handover (ISBAR).

Gives oxygen for the low SpO2 (91% in room air), titrated to the target range the neonatal team uses for a term baby, and escalates respiratory support (CPAP) if the baby tires, has apnoea or needs more oxygen.
Obtains IV or IO access and gives 0.9% sodium chloride 10 mL/kg = 32 mL for 3.2 kg, reassesses HR and CRT, and repeats 10 mL/kg (32 mL) if still shocked.
Takes a blood culture without delaying treatment, then gives IV benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg = 192 mg for 3.2 kg (12-hourly) and gentamicin 5 mg/kg = 16 mg for 3.2 kg (24-hourly) straight away.
Starts maintenance IV fluid with 10% glucose at 60 mL/kg/day on day 1 = 8 mL/h for 3.2 kg, and plans repeat BGLs.
Admits to the neonatal unit with continuous monitoring, plans a lumbar puncture once stable, repeats the CRP, and reviews antibiotics at 36 hours with the culture result and the baby's condition.

Explains to the mother in plain language that the baby probably has a blood and lung infection, needs antibiotics, oxygen and fluids in the neonatal unit, that GBS carriage is common and not her fault, and that she can stay close and express breast milk.
Safety netting
States the triggers for urgent senior review in the unit: apnoea or a rising oxygen need, shock signs returning after two boluses (inotropes are then considered), a low BGL, or seizures.

Tells the parents that after discharge they should return to the ED, or call 000 if the baby is floppy, blue or not breathing normally, for poor feeding, sleepiness, a temperature of 38 °C or more or a low temperature, fast or noisy breathing, or fewer wet nappies, because late-onset GBS infection can occur in the first 3 months.

Arranges follow-up: GP and maternal and child health review after discharge, and tells the mother that if GBS infection is confirmed she should be offered antibiotics in labour in any future pregnancy, so her next maternity team must know.

part2.lead: Here is the reassessment 20 minutes later, on oxygen and after one 10 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride, and the first results. The blood culture was taken before antibiotics.

handover.label: Observations and reassessment 20 minutes later
handover.result: Since 22:45: low-flow oxygen by nasal prongs and one 10 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride (32 mL).

rows.note: Grunting, mottled and floppy; not feeding
After the bolus: less grunting; blood culture taken

handover.model:
At 22:40 nearly every value is abnormal for a term newborn: HR 188 and RR 74 are above the RCH acceptable ranges (HR 120 to 170, RR 25 to 60), SpO2 91% in air is low, CRT is 4 seconds with mottling, the temperature is 38.1 °C and the baby responds to voice only. Systolic 58 is just under the acceptable range (60 to 95); BP falls late in a newborn, so with the tachycardia and poor perfusion this is shock needing fluid now. With grunting and moderate distress, this is sepsis with shock and respiratory distress; the BGL of 4.1 is normal.

At 23:00, on 0.5 L/min oxygen and after one 10 mL/kg bolus, SpO2 95%, HR 164, CRT 2 seconds and BP 62/36 show a response, but RR 66, the fever and a baby still responding only to voice mean the baby remains unwell. Keep reassessing HR and CRT (a second 10 mL/kg if shock signs return), keep the BGL at 2.6 mmol/L or above (3.9 now), and the neonatal team stays at the cot side: apnoea, a rising oxygen need or shock after two boluses needs urgent senior review.

handover.label: Venous blood gas
handover.result: Venous sample, 22:50, at cannulation with the blood culture, before the bolus.
handover.model:
pH 7.24 is an acidaemia; bicarbonate 17 and base excess -9 make it metabolic, and the lactate of 4.2 mmol/L (anion gap about 16) shows a lactic acidosis from poor tissue perfusion in septic shock. The venous pCO2 of 40 is the expected respiratory compensation: for a bicarbonate of 17, Winters' formula predicts an arterial pCO2 of about 32 to 36, and venous blood runs a few mmHg higher, so there is no respiratory acidosis yet. Sodium, potassium, chloride and glucose are normal.

It changes the urgency, not the treatment: fluid, oxygen and antibiotics now, then a repeat gas to see the lactate fall. A baby breathing at 74 with grunting and pneumonia can tire, so a rising pCO2 on the repeat gas, apnoea or a rising oxygen need means the neonatal team starts respiratory support (CPAP).

handover.label: Full blood examination and CRP
handover.result:
Taken at 22:50 with the blood culture, about 14 hours of age.

Film: toxic granulation and vacuolation of the neutrophils. No blasts. Platelets slightly reduced, no clumping.
handover.model:
The white cell count is low (3.1) with neutropenia (total neutrophils 1.4, of which 0.4 are band forms) and lymphopenia (1.4). The immature to total neutrophil ratio is 0.4 / 1.4 = 0.29, above 0.20, and the film shows toxic changes: in a newborn with shock this is the marrow's neutrophil reserve being used up by overwhelming infection, a worrying sign and not a reassuring one. Platelets of 140 are slightly low (consumption in sepsis); the haemoglobin is normal.

A CRP of 6 mg/L is barely raised, but CRP takes 12 to 24 hours to rise, and a newborn's CRP also drifts up a little over the first 2 days without infection, so one early value means little either way: repeat it in 12 to 24 hours and treat now on the clinical picture. Together they support early-onset sepsis and add to the case for neonatal unit care.

handover.label: Chest X-ray
handover.result:
Chest X-ray, AP supine, single view, 23:10.

Clinical details: 14-hour-old term baby with grunting, tachypnoea, fever and an oxygen requirement. Sepsis? Pneumonia?

Findings:

  • Lines and tubes: none.
  • Lungs: bilateral diffuse hazy (ground-glass) opacification with air bronchograms. No focal collapse. No fluid in the fissures.
  • Pleura: no pneumothorax or pleural effusion.
  • Heart and mediastinum: normal heart size and shape. Normal thymic shadow.
  • Bones and upper abdomen: normal. Stomach bubble on the left, normal bowel gas pattern.

Conclusion: bilateral hazy opacification with air bronchograms, consistent with pneumonia in this clinical setting; surfactant deficiency can look the same but is uncommon at term. No pneumothorax.
handover.model:
An adequate AP supine film with no lines: bilateral diffuse hazy opacification with air bronchograms, a normal heart size and no pneumothorax or effusion. In a febrile term baby with maternal GBS carriage, membranes ruptured 20 hours and a maternal fever, this is pneumonia from early-onset sepsis, most likely GBS, until proven otherwise; GBS pneumonia can look identical to surfactant deficiency, and transient tachypnoea would not explain the fever and shock.

No pneumothorax and a normal heart size are reassuring, though a normal film does not exclude duct-dependent heart disease. It confirms the need for oxygen and a close watch for tiring (CPAP if needed) and does not change the antibiotics.

handover.label: Blood culture and lumbar puncture
handover.result:
SpecimenCollectedReport
Blood culture, aerobic paediatric bottle, 1 mL22:50, before antibioticsIncubating: no growth to date. Positive results are phoned through; final report at 5 days.
Cerebrospinal fluid (lumbar puncture)Not yet collectedNo specimen received.
handover.model:
No growth yet means nothing: the culture was taken minutes ago, and most bacteraemia in newborns is detected within 36 hours, which is why the RCH guideline reviews antibiotics at 36 hours with the culture result and the baby's condition. Taking 1 mL before antibiotics was right, and the antibiotics must not wait for it.

The lumbar puncture has not been done: defer it while the baby is unstable (oxygen requirement, shock) and do it once stable (CSF cell count, protein, glucose, Gram stain, culture and PCR). If meningitis is suspected or the CSF is abnormal, the RCH guideline changes to benzylpenicillin with a third-generation cephalosporin. With shock, neutropenia and pneumonia, antibiotics are unlikely to stop at 36 hours even if the culture stays negative.

ask: You are now calling the neonatal registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of this baby, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of this baby now, here on the postnatal ward.
Before this baby goes home, what would you tell the parents and what follow-up would you arrange?
expect:
• Identify: self, postnatal ward; 14-hour-old term baby, 3.2 kg.
  • Situation: suspected early-onset sepsis with shock and respiratory distress; I need you here now.
  • Background: 38+5, normal vaginal birth, Apgars 9 and 9. Mother GBS positive, membranes ruptured 20 h, one dose of benzylpenicillin 2 h before birth, maternal fever 38.2 °C. Poor feeding from 10 h, grunting for 2 h.
  • Assessment: at 22:40 HR 188, RR 74, SpO2 91% in air, CRT 4 s, BP 58/30, 38.1 °C, responds to voice, BGL 4.1. After oxygen and a 32 mL bolus, improved but still unwell. VBG: metabolic lactic acidosis, compensated for now. Neutropenia, I:T ratio 0.29, toxic film: worrying. CRP 6: too early to exclude sepsis. CXR: pneumonia. Blood culture taken.
  • Recommendation: come now and arrange a NICU bed; advise on antibiotics, a second bolus and CPAP.

Most likely: early-onset neonatal sepsis, probably GBS, with pneumonia and septic shock. Supported by maternal GBS carriage, inadequate intrapartum antibiotics, membranes ruptured 20 h, maternal fever; fever, grunting, HR 188, CRT 4 s, lactate 4.2, neutropenia with toxic changes, bilateral hazy CXR.

  • Transient tachypnoea: against: fever, shock, onset after 10 h.
  • Surfactant deficiency: CXR can look the same, but uncommon at term and does not explain fever or neutropenia.
  • Duct-dependent congenital heart disease: heart size normal and fluid helped, but a normal film does not exclude it; check pre- and post-ductal SpO2.
  • Inborn error of metabolism: glucose normal and perfusion explains the lactate; check ammonia if not improving.

None of these should delay antibiotics.

1. Neonatal team at the cot side; continuous monitoring.
  2. Oxygen titrated to the term target range; CPAP if tiring, apnoea, rising oxygen need or rising pCO2.
  3. IV or IO access; reassess HR and CRT; repeat 0.9% sodium chloride 10 mL/kg = 32 mL if shock returns.
  4. Blood culture taken, then straight away IV benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg = 192 mg 12-hourly and gentamicin 5 mg/kg = 16 mg 24-hourly.
  5. 10% glucose at 60 mL/kg/day = 8 mL/h; repeat BGLs, keep 2.6 mmol/L or above.
  6. Admit to NICU. Repeat the gas and the CRP in 12 to 24 h; lumbar puncture once stable (switch to benzylpenicillin plus a third-generation cephalosporin if meningitis is suspected); review antibiotics at 36 h.
  7. Urgent senior review for apnoea, a rising oxygen need, shock after two boluses (consider inotropes), a low BGL or seizures.
  8. Tell the mother plainly: blood and lung infection; GBS carriage is common and not her fault; she can stay close and express breast milk.

Call 000 if the baby is floppy, blue or not breathing normally.

Come straight to the ED for:

  • poor feeding or being unusually sleepy;
  • a temperature of 38 °C or more, or a low temperature;
  • fast or noisy breathing;
  • fewer wet nappies.

Explain why: late-onset GBS infection can happen in the first 3 months.

Follow-up:

  • GP and maternal and child health nurse review soon after discharge, with a discharge summary.
  • If GBS infection is confirmed, the mother should be offered antibiotics in labour in any future pregnancy. She should tell her next maternity team.
